uses.paragraph:
Miller's construction gives a sequence $a\in Q$ with the following
property: if an oracle program with index $d$ computes the same real $r\in[0,1]$ from
every $p\in P_a$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:miller-property}
 a(d)=r.
\end{equation}
Such a sequence is called a \emph{Miller sequence}
\cite[Theorem~2.2]{BauerHanson}.
The index equality is the strengthened conclusion stated after
\cite[Theorem~6.3]{Miller2004}; the formulation with binary
representations is given in
\cite[Section~2.1 and Theorem~2.2]{BauerHanson}.
The rational approximations produced by $d$ may depend on $p$,
while the real they represent is fixed.

Miller constructed a sequence that enumerates every real in $[0,1]$
computable uniformly from its representations \cite[Theorem~6.3]{Miller2004}.
We use the stronger index property stated immediately after that
theorem and recalled in Section~\ref{sec:miller}.
Bauer and Hanson use this construction in a parameterized realizability
topos with countable Dedekind reals \cite{BauerHanson}.
Section~\ref{sec:miller} uses their binary representations to construct a recursion category,
prove inseparability of $L_a,R_a$, and obtain essential incompleteness
for a theory of real closed fields.

uses.paragraph:
Bernardi's numerical argument uses a precomplete equivalence
relation $R$ on $\N$: for every partial recursive function $f$
there is a total recursive function $g$ such that
$f(n)\mathord\downarrow$ implies $f(n)\,R\,g(n)$.
For such a relation, distinct equivalence classes are recursively
inseparable; consequently the same holds for disjoint nonempty
unions of classes. The relation $\equiv_{\PA}$ on indices defined
in \eqref{eq:uniform} is one of his examples
\cite[pp.~125--126]{Bernardi}.
The argument above obtains $A,B$ from
Corollary~\ref{cor:source-conditionals} and uses finite PA-proofs to
establish $A\subseteq P_T$ and $B\subseteq N_T$.

Di Paola and Heller proved recursive inseparability in dominical
recursion categories in which every morphism has a section
\cite[Theorem 8.15]{DPH}. Bernardi obtained categorical inseparability
results from precomplete equivalence relations, including PA-provable
equality of partial recursive functions among his examples
\cite[pp.~125--128]{Bernardi}.
Montagna also obtained effectively inseparable pairs in his syntactic
category $S$
\cite[Remark 3.1]{Montagna}.

uses.paragraph:
Di Paola and Heller introduced dominical categories as a setting for
recursion theory \cite{DPH}. Rosolini's $P$-categories generalized this
setting \cite{RosoliniThesis,Rosolini}. Heller adopted them and defined
prodominical categories \cite[Section 5]{Heller}.
Cockett and Lack introduced restriction categories \cite{CockettLack},
and Cockett and Hofstra developed the theory of Turing categories
\cite{CockettHofstra}. We use restriction categories, with binary
restriction products in the source recursion categories. These products
give the equivalent $P$-category structure
\cite[Proposition 4.5]{CockettLackIII}.

For a restriction category $\mathcal R$, its restriction splitting
$\Split(\mathcal R)$ has objects $(X,e)$, where $e=\bar e$, and
morphisms $f:(X,e)\rightharpoonup(Y,d)$ satisfying $f=dfe$.
Its identity on $(X,e)$ is $e$; such a morphism is total when
$\bar f=e$. Write $\Tot(\Split(\mathcal R))$ for the subcategory
of total morphisms~\cite[Section 2.3.3]{CockettLack}.

The partial-map category $\Par(\mathcal D,\Mono)$ has morphisms given
by spans with monic left leg, composed by pullback
\cite[Section 3]{CockettLack}. Since $\mathcal D$ is regular, it is a
split restriction category with ranges
\cite[Theorem 4.5 and Section 4.11]{CGHRangeI}; its total subcategory
is canonically isomorphic to $\mathcal D$.
The sentence theory is represented in this category by
\[
 t_A=[S\xleftarrow{m_A}T_{A,S}\xrightarrow{m_A}S]:S\rightharpoonup S,
 \qquad m_A:T_{A,S}\hookrightarrow S.
\]
Every monomorphism in $\mathcal D$ has a partial inverse in this
partial-map category. Lemma~\ref{lem:range-regular-image} therefore
gives $t_A=\ran(c_{A,S})$.
If instead $\mathcal D=\Tot(\Split(\mathcal R))$ for a restriction
category $\mathcal R$ whose restriction splitting has ranges, require
$m_A$ to have a partial inverse
$r_A:S\rightharpoonup T_{A,S}$ in $\Split(\mathcal R)$.
The same lemma gives
\[
 \ran(c_{A,S})=m_A r_A=\bar r_A.
\]
Thus the range represents the constructed sentence theory.

Composition is written $gf=g\circ f$, so $f$ is applied first.
A \emph{restriction category} is a category equipped with an assignment
that sends every morphism
$f:X\rightharpoonup Y$ to a morphism
$\bar f:X\rightharpoonup X$ satisfying
\[
 f\bar f=f,\qquad
 \bar f\bar g=\bar g\bar f,\qquad
 \overline{g\bar f}=\bar g\bar f,\qquad
 \bar h f=f\overline{hf}.
\]
In the middle two equations $g:X\rightharpoonup Z$; in the last,
$h:Y\rightharpoonup Z$ \cite{CockettLack}.
The morphisms $\bar f$ are idempotent and are called
\emph{restriction idempotents}, also called domains
\cite[Section~5]{Heller}.
The morphism $f$ is \emph{total} when $\bar f=1_X$.
The total morphisms form a subcategory, denoted by
$\operatorname{Tot}(\mathcal C)$ for a restriction category $\mathcal C$.
A \emph{restriction functor} $F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ between
restriction categories satisfies $F(\bar f)=\overline{F(f)}$ for every
morphism $f$. A \emph{restriction equivalence} consists of restriction
functors in both directions whose composites are naturally isomorphic
to the respective identity functors.

A restriction idempotent $e$ on $X$ \emph{splits} if
$e=mr$ for a total $m:A\to X$ and $r:X\rightharpoonup A$
with $rm=1_A$. The category is \emph{split} when every restriction
idempotent splits.
For a restriction category $\mathcal C$, write
$\operatorname{Split}(\mathcal C)$ for the category obtained from
$\mathcal C$ by splitting the restriction idempotents of $\mathcal C$.
Cockett--Lack denote this category by $K_r(\mathcal C)$
\cite[Section~2.3.3]{CockettLack}.
The objects of $\operatorname{Split}(\mathcal C)$ are pairs $(X,e)$, where $e$ is a
restriction idempotent on $X$, and morphisms
$f:(X,e)\rightharpoonup(Y,d)$ given by original morphisms
$f:X\rightharpoonup Y$ satisfying $f=dfe$.
The identity of $(X,e)$ is $e$, and $f$ is total there when
$\bar f=e$. Thus $(X,e)$ is the object through which $e$ splits.

The \emph{Karoubi envelope} $\operatorname{Kar}(\mathcal C)$ has the
same description with arbitrary idempotents $e:X\rightharpoonup X$
in place of restriction idempotents. The restriction operation on
$\operatorname{Kar}(\mathcal C)$ sends
$f:(X,e)\rightharpoonup(Y,d)$ to the morphism represented by $\bar f e$.
This is the construction $K_E(\mathcal C)$ of
\cite[Section~2.3.3, Proposition~2.26]{CockettLack} with $E$ the class
of all idempotents.

uses.paragraph:
A \emph{binary restriction product} $X\times Y$ has total
projections $\pi_1:X\times Y\to X$ and $\pi_2:X\times Y\to Y$.
For morphisms $f:Z\rightharpoonup X$ and $g:Z\rightharpoonup Y$,
there is a unique $\langle f,g\rangle:Z\rightharpoonup X\times Y$
with
\[
 \pi_1\langle f,g\rangle=f\bar g,\qquad
 \pi_2\langle f,g\rangle=g\bar f,\qquad
 \overline{\langle f,g\rangle}=\bar f\bar g.
\]
Products of morphisms are obtained by this pairing and the projections.
The total categorical diagonal is
$\Delta_X=\langle1_X,1_X\rangle:X\to X\times X$.
A restriction category has a $P$-category structure if and only if
it has binary restriction products
\cite[Proposition 4.5]{CockettLackIII}.

uses.paragraph:
For a topological space $X$, let $\mathcal O(X)$ be the category
of open sets and inclusions. A \emph{set-valued cosheaf} is a
covariant functor $C:\mathcal O(X)\to\mathbf{Set}$ for which
every open cover $(O_\lambda)_\lambda$ of $O$ gives a coequalizer
\cite[Definition 2.6]{CurryCosheaves}
\[
 \coprod_{\lambda,\mu} C(O_\lambda\cap O_\mu)
 \rightrightarrows \coprod_\lambda C(O_\lambda)
 \longrightarrow C(O).
\]
The two parallel maps are induced by the inclusions into the two
members of the cover; the empty cover requires
$C(\varnothing)=\varnothing$.
The \emph{Sierpi\'nski space} has two points and exactly three open
sets: the empty set, one singleton, and the whole space.

uses.paragraph:
For consistent computably enumerable $T\supseteq\PA$, the source $S_T$
is not locally connected \cite[Corollary 4.4, pp.~657--658]{DPM}.
The connected restriction idempotents used in the preceding proof
belong to $\mathcal D_T$ and need not be images of source restriction
idempotents.

Use the deterministic computation coding for Kleene's trace
predicate as in \cite[p.~115, Note~1]{Montagna}.
Let $e,x,t$ range over $\N$, and write
$\mathsf{Tr}(e,x,t)$ for the primitive-recursive predicate
that $t$ is a halting computation trace with index $e$ and input
$x$, and let $\mathsf{out}:\N\to\N$ be the primitive-recursive
output-extraction function. Put
\[
 G(e,x,y)\equiv
 \exists t\,\bigl(\mathsf{Tr}(e,x,t)\land\mathsf{out}(t)=y\bigr),
 \qquad G_e(x,y)=G(\bar e,x,y).
\]
Primitive-recursive symbols abbreviate their defining formulas in
PA, as in \cite[p.~644]{DPM}; the expanded graph formula is $\Sigma_1$.
For $X,Y\in\mathsf O$, let $\mathcal I(X,Y)=\N$.
An index $e\in\mathcal I(X,Y)$ is interpreted using
$\gamma_X$ for inputs and $\gamma_Y$ for outputs.

Montagna's objects are the sets generated from $\N$ by
Cartesian products and the displayed disjoint unions
\cite[p.~105]{Montagna}. Let $S_T^{\mathrm{set}}$ denote that
presentation of the unprimed category, using the computation
formulas and the induced numerical codings fixed above
\cite{Montagna,DPM}. There is a functor
\[
 \Pi_T:S_T\longrightarrow S_T^{\mathrm{set}},\qquad
 \Pi_T(X)=|X|,\qquad \Pi_T([e]_T)=[e]_T^{\mathrm{set}}.
\]
Every object of $S_T^{\mathrm{set}}$ is $|X|$ for a term
$X\in\mathsf O$, and the map on each hom-set is a bijection
because both presentations use \eqref{eq:uniform} with the same
numerical codings. Thus $\Pi_T$ is an equivalence. For $T=\PA$,
the target is Montagna's unprimed category $S$ with these choices
of computation formulas and codings.

The pointwise relation used in the primed systems identifies
$e,f\in\mathcal I(X,Y)$ when, for every standard input code $n$,
\[
 T\vdash\forall y\,
   \bigl(G_e(\bar n,y)\leftrightarrow G_f(\bar n,y)\bigr).
\]
Montagna's $S'$ is the case
$T=\PA$ of Di Paola and Montagna's $S'_T$ \cite{Montagna,DPM}.
\emph{Pointwise provable equality and the failure of composition}
\cite[Corollary 2]{Composition} proves that the proposed composition
is not independent of representatives for any consistent c.e.\
extension $T$ of $\PA$. Thus these primed systems do not define
categories with that composition.

We also apply the criterion to the syntactic recursion categories of
Montagna and Di Paola--Montagna \cite{Montagna,DPM}.
For a consistent computably enumerable (c.e.)
extension $T$ of Peano arithmetic ($\PA$), the morphisms of $S_T$ are
equivalence classes of indices of partial recursive functions. Two
indices are identified when $T$ proves the universal closure of the
equivalence of their graph formulas. These categories are not locally
connected \cite[Corollary 4.4]{DPM}. Interpretation in all models of
$T$ with carrier $\N$ gives a faithful range functor into a locally
connected product of partial-map categories. Partial recursive functions
selecting between predicates proved complementary in $T$ represent the
required section lifts.
The construction commutes with theory extension.
The total restriction splitting of $S_T$ also realizes the
first-order syntax and theory construction of
Appendix~\ref{app:syntax-theories}
(Theorem~\ref{thm:syntactic-generated-theory}).
Its universal properties use $T$-provable graph equality.

A \emph{restriction category} is a category equipped with an assignment
that sends every morphism
$f:X\rightharpoonup Y$ to a morphism
$\bar f:X\rightharpoonup X$ satisfying
\[
 f\bar f=f,\qquad
 \bar f\bar g=\bar g\bar f,\qquad
 \overline{g\bar f}=\bar g\bar f,\qquad
 \bar h f=f\overline{hf}.
\]
In the middle two equations $g:X\rightharpoonup Z$; in the last,
$h:Y\rightharpoonup Z$ \cite{CockettLack}.
The morphisms $\bar f$ are idempotent and are called
\emph{restriction idempotents}, also called domains
\cite[Section~5]{Heller}.
The morphism $f$ is \emph{total} when $\bar f=1_X$.
The total morphisms form a subcategory, denoted by
$\operatorname{Tot}(\mathcal C)$ for a restriction category $\mathcal C$.
A \emph{restriction functor} $F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ between
restriction categories satisfies $F(\bar f)=\overline{F(f)}$ for every
morphism $f$. A \emph{restriction equivalence} consists of restriction
functors in both directions whose composites are naturally isomorphic
to the respective identity functors.

For $f:X\rightharpoonup Y$ and a restriction idempotent $a$ on $Y$,
the \emph{inverse image} of $a$ is the restriction idempotent
$f^*a=\overline{af}$ on $X$.
A restriction idempotent $r$ on $Y$ \emph{receives} $f$ when $rf=f$
\cite[Section 6]{Heller}.
The \emph{range} $\ran(f)$ is the least restriction idempotent receiving $f$;
we require the agreement law
\[
 gf=hf\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 g\ran(f)=h\ran(f)
 \qquad(g,h:Y\rightharpoonup Z).
\]
For an ordinary partial function $f$, the restriction idempotent
$\bar f$ and the range $\ran(f)$ are the partial identities on its
domain of definition and image, respectively.

A \emph{Turing morphism} on $U$ is a morphism
$\tau:U\times U\rightharpoonup U$ such that, for every object $X$
and every $f:X\times U\rightharpoonup U$, there is a total
parameter map $r:X\to U$ satisfying
\[
 f=\tau(r\times1_U).
\]
A \emph{recursion category} here is a prodominical isotypical
category with binary restriction products and a Turing morphism,
as in \cite[Section 9]{Heller}.

Define an object $V:J\to\mathcal C_{\mathrm{rec}}$ of $\mathcal E$
by the following objects $V_j=V(j)$ and morphisms
$r_i^V=V(0\to i)$:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:universal-fork}
 \begin{gathered}
 V_0=\N^4,\qquad V_1=V_2=\N^2,\\
 r_1^V:V_0\to V_1,\qquad r_1^V(k,z,a,b)=(k,a),\\
 r_2^V:V_0\to V_2,\qquad r_2^V(k,z,a,b)=(k,b).
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
We regard $V$ also as an object of $\mathcal A$, whose objects
are those of $\mathcal E$.
For an object $A=(m,A_0)$ of $\mathcal C_{\mathrm{rec}}$, put
$m(A)=m$. Thus $|A|\subseteq\N^{m(A)}$,
$m(V_0)=4$, and $m(V_1)=m(V_2)=2$.
Fix recursive numerical encodings of nonempty finite sequences of tuples,
\[
 \operatorname{code}_m:
 \coprod_{n\ge1}(\N^m)^n\xrightarrow{\cong}W_m\subseteq\N
 \qquad(m\ge0),
\]
where each $W_m$ is recursive and the length and entry operations
are recursive. For an object $A$ of $\mathcal C_{\mathrm{rec}}$, put
\[
 A^\#=\{\operatorname{code}_{m(A)}(a_1,\ldots,a_n):
                 n\ge1,\ a_1,\ldots,a_n\in A\}\subseteq W_{m(A)}.
\]
This is a c.e.\ numerical carrier. Let $V^\#$ have components
$(V^\#)_j=(V_j)^\#$.
Its map $(V^\#)(0\to i):(V_0)^\#\to(V_i)^\#$ decodes a sequence,
applies $r_i^V$ to each entry, and encodes the resulting sequence,
for $i=1,2$.
Choose isomorphisms in $\mathcal E$
$V\cong V\times V$, $V\cong V+V$, and $V\cong V^\#$.
Together with their inverses, these form a \emph{frame} at $V$
\cite[Section 3]{Heller}.
Let $\mathscr R_X$ denote the full subcategory of $\mathcal A$
on the objects obtained from $V$ by finitely many applications of
the chosen binary restriction products, binary coproducts, and
nonempty-word formation.
The isomorphisms, constructed in Lemma~\ref{lem:fork-frames}, make
$\mathscr R_X$ isotypical.

uses.paragraph:
Miller's construction gives a sequence $a\in Q$ with the following
property: if an oracle program with index $d$ computes the same real $r\in[0,1]$ from
every $p\in P_a$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:miller-property}
 a(d)=r.
\end{equation}
Such a sequence is called a \emph{Miller sequence}
\cite[Theorem~2.2]{BauerHanson}.
The index equality is the strengthened conclusion stated after
\cite[Theorem~6.3]{Miller2004}; the formulation with binary
representations is given in
\cite[Section~2.1 and Theorem~2.2]{BauerHanson}.
The rational approximations produced by $d$ may depend on $p$,
while the real they represent is fixed.

The principal application uses a sequence $a:\N\to[0,1]$ constructed
by Miller \cite{Miller2004}. We form a category $\mathcal E_a$ whose
morphisms are partial numerical functions computed by one oracle program
with the same domain and values for every binary representation of $a$.
Compactness of the set of representations permits the construction of a Turing
morphism in this category. The index sets
\[
 L_a=\{n:a(n)<1/2\},\qquad R_a=\{n:a(n)>1/2\}
\]
are semidecidable in $\mathcal E_a$. We construct an ordinary recursive
map reducing the diagonal pair of Corollary~\ref{cor:source-conditionals} to
$L_a,R_a$, and hence prove their inseparability in $\mathcal E_a$.
Each fixed binary representation $p$ computes a separator of $L_a$
and $R_a$. The inclusion into the recursion category of
$p$-partial recursive functions is a faithful range functor preserving
restriction products and sends this inseparable pair to a separable pair.

Miller constructed a sequence that enumerates every real in $[0,1]$
computable uniformly from its representations \cite[Theorem~6.3]{Miller2004}.
We use the stronger index property stated immediately after that
theorem and recalled in Section~\ref{sec:miller}.
Bauer and Hanson use this construction in a parameterized realizability
topos with countable Dedekind reals \cite{BauerHanson}.
Section~\ref{sec:miller} uses their binary representations to construct a recursion category,
prove inseparability of $L_a,R_a$, and obtain essential incompleteness
for a theory of real closed fields.

uses.paragraph:
Use the deterministic computation coding for Kleene's trace
predicate as in \cite[p.~115, Note~1]{Montagna}.
Let $e,x,t$ range over $\N$, and write
$\mathsf{Tr}(e,x,t)$ for the primitive-recursive predicate
that $t$ is a halting computation trace with index $e$ and input
$x$, and let $\mathsf{out}:\N\to\N$ be the primitive-recursive
output-extraction function. Put
\[
 G(e,x,y)\equiv
 \exists t\,\bigl(\mathsf{Tr}(e,x,t)\land\mathsf{out}(t)=y\bigr),
 \qquad G_e(x,y)=G(\bar e,x,y).
\]
Primitive-recursive symbols abbreviate their defining formulas in
PA, as in \cite[p.~644]{DPM}; the expanded graph formula is $\Sigma_1$.
For $X,Y\in\mathsf O$, let $\mathcal I(X,Y)=\N$.
An index $e\in\mathcal I(X,Y)$ is interpreted using
$\gamma_X$ for inputs and $\gamma_Y$ for outputs.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:arithmetized-evaluation}
For this computation coding, there are an index $u\in\N$ and
primitive-recursive functions
$\operatorname{s},\operatorname{comp}:\N^2\to\N$
such that PA proves functionality
of $G$ and the universal closures of
\begin{align}
 G_u(\langle e,x\rangle,y)
   &\leftrightarrow G(e,x,y),
   \label{eq:arithmetized-universal}\\
 G(\operatorname{s}(e,a),x,y)
   &\leftrightarrow G(e,\langle a,x\rangle,y),
   \label{eq:arithmetized-specialization}\\
 G(\operatorname{comp}(f,e),x,z)
   &\leftrightarrow
     \exists y\,\bigl(G(e,x,y)\land G(f,y,z)\bigr).
   \label{eq:composition}
\end{align}
Regard $u$ as an element of $\mathcal I(\omega\times\omega,\omega)$.
For each fixed $e\in\N$, there is an index
$k_e\in\N$ for which PA proves
\[
 \forall a\forall p\,
 \bigl(G_{k_e}(a,p)\leftrightarrow
       p=\operatorname{s}(\bar e,a)\bigr).
\]
In particular, PA proves $\forall a\exists!p\,G_{k_e}(a,p)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
These are the formalized enumeration, composition, and
parameterization properties of the computation coding used in
\cite[p.~108; p.~115, Note~1]{Montagna}.
The pairing can be replaced by the pairing fixed above, using
the PA-provable inverse equations for the two numerical codings.
For $k_e$, use an index for the primitive-recursive function
$a\mapsto\operatorname{s}(e,a)$; its defining equation and
totality are provable in PA.
\end{proof}

Montagna's objects are the sets generated from $\N$ by
Cartesian products and the displayed disjoint unions
\cite[p.~105]{Montagna}. Let $S_T^{\mathrm{set}}$ denote that
presentation of the unprimed category, using the computation
formulas and the induced numerical codings fixed above
\cite{Montagna,DPM}. There is a functor
\[
 \Pi_T:S_T\longrightarrow S_T^{\mathrm{set}},\qquad
 \Pi_T(X)=|X|,\qquad \Pi_T([e]_T)=[e]_T^{\mathrm{set}}.
\]
Every object of $S_T^{\mathrm{set}}$ is $|X|$ for a term
$X\in\mathsf O$, and the map on each hom-set is a bijection
because both presentations use \eqref{eq:uniform} with the same
numerical codings. Thus $\Pi_T$ is an equivalence. For $T=\PA$,
the target is Montagna's unprimed category $S$ with these choices
of computation formulas and codings.

Cartesian products and the displayed disjoint unions
\cite[p.~105]{Montagna}. Let $S_T^{\mathrm{set}}$ denote that
presentation of the unprimed category, using the computation
formulas and the induced numerical codings fixed above
\cite{Montagna,DPM}. There is a functor
\[

 \Pi_T(X)=|X|,\qquad \Pi_T([e]_T)=[e]_T^{\mathrm{set}}.
\]
Every object of $S_T^{\mathrm{set}}$ is $|X|$ for a term
$X\in\mathsf O$, and the map on each hom-set is a bijection
because both presentations use \eqref{eq:uniform} with the same
numerical codings. Thus $\Pi_T$ is an equivalence. For $T=\PA$,
the target is Montagna's unprimed category $S$ with these choices
of computation formulas and codings.

The pointwise relation used in the primed systems identifies
$e,f\in\mathcal I(X,Y)$ when, for every standard input code $n$,
\[
 T\vdash\forall y\,
   \bigl(G_e(\bar n,y)\leftrightarrow G_f(\bar n,y)\bigr).
\]
Montagna's $S'$ is the case
$T=\PA$ of Di Paola and Montagna's $S'_T$ \cite{Montagna,DPM}.
\emph{Pointwise provable equality and the failure of composition}
\cite[Corollary 2]{Composition} proves that the proposed composition
is not independent of representatives for any consistent c.e.\
extension $T$ of $\PA$. Thus these primed systems do not define
categories with that composition.

For $X\in\mathsf O$ and a $\Sigma_1$ arithmetic formula $C(x)$,
where $x$ is the numerical code variable for $X$, choose
a witness-search index $j_C$ for which
\[
 \PA\vdash\forall x\forall y\,
 \bigl(G_{j_C}(x,y)\leftrightarrow(C(x)\land y=x)\bigr).
\]
Such an index searches increasing bounds for a witness to $C(x)$
and returns $x$ when a witness is found
\cite[p.~109, equation~$(*)$]{Montagna}. Write
$[C]_T=[j_C]_T:X\rightharpoonup X$.
For two such formulas,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:domain-order}
 [C]_T\le[D]_T
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 T\vdash\forall x\,(C(x)\longrightarrow D(x)).
\end{equation}
Conjunction and disjunction give meets and joins of restriction
idempotents. For $[e]_T:X\rightharpoonup Y$, its restriction
$\overline{[e]_T}$ and range $\ran([e]_T)$ are represented respectively by
\[
 \exists y\,G_e(x,y),\qquad
 R_e(y):=\exists x\,G_e(x,y).
\]
For a restriction idempotent $[C]_T:Y\rightharpoonup Y$, the
equation $[C]_T[e]_T=[e]_T$ holds precisely when
$T$ proves $G_e(x,y)\to C(y)$ universally, equivalently when
$T$ proves $R_e(y)\to C(y)$ universally.
Write $g=[p]_T,h=[q]_T:Y\rightharpoonup Z$.
If $g[e]_T=h[e]_T$, the
composition equation and PA-provable functionality of $G_e$ give
\[
 T\vdash\forall y\forall z\,
 \bigl(R_e(y)\longrightarrow
       (G_p(y,z)\leftrightarrow G_q(y,z))\bigr).
\]
Indeed, a witness $x$ to $R_e(y)$ can be used in the equality of
the composite graphs, and functionality identifies the intermediate
output with $y$. This proves $g[R_e]_T=h[R_e]_T$ in $S_T$.
The index $j_{R_e}$ is independent of the theory, so its class
represents the range over every extension of $T$.

We also apply the criterion to the syntactic recursion categories of
Montagna and Di Paola--Montagna \cite{Montagna,DPM}.
For a consistent computably enumerable (c.e.)
extension $T$ of Peano arithmetic ($\PA$), the morphisms of $S_T$ are
equivalence classes of indices of partial recursive functions. Two
indices are identified when $T$ proves the universal closure of the
equivalence of their graph formulas. These categories are not locally
connected \cite[Corollary 4.4]{DPM}. Interpretation in all models of
$T$ with carrier $\N$ gives a faithful range functor into a locally
connected product of partial-map categories. Partial recursive functions
selecting between predicates proved complementary in $T$ represent the
required section lifts.
The construction commutes with theory extension.
The total restriction splitting of $S_T$ also realizes the
first-order syntax and theory construction of
Appendix~\ref{app:syntax-theories}
(Theorem~\ref{thm:syntactic-generated-theory}).
Its universal properties use $T$-provable graph equality.

Di Paola and Heller proved recursive inseparability in dominical
recursion categories in which every morphism has a section
\cite[Theorem 8.15]{DPH}. Bernardi obtained categorical inseparability
results from precomplete equivalence relations, including PA-provable
equality of partial recursive functions among his examples
\cite[pp.~125--128]{Bernardi}.
Montagna also obtained effectively inseparable pairs in his syntactic
category $S$
\cite[Remark 3.1]{Montagna}.

uses.paragraph:
Aczel~\cite[Propositions 1.1.4 and 1.4.5]{Aczel} describes finitary
inductive closure by the conclusions of finite proofs. We express the
rule presentation in a slice category.
Let $\mathcal D$ be regular with finite coproducts, and fix an object
$F$. For an integer $N\geq0$, let
\[
 p_n:R_n\longrightarrow F^n,\qquad
 q_n:R_n\longrightarrow F\quad(0\leq n\leq N)
\]
specify rule instances, their ordered premises, and their conclusions.
The nullary rule instances specify axioms.
For an object $q:Q\to F$ of the slice category $\mathcal D/F$,
form the pullback
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
 B_n(Q,q)\arrow[r,"{b_{n,q}}"]\arrow[d,"{a_{n,q}}"'] &
 Q^n\arrow[d,"q^n"]\\
 R_n\arrow[r,"p_n"'] & F^n.
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Put
\[
 H(Q,q)=\left(\coprod_{n=0}^N B_n(Q,q),\kappa_q\right),\qquad
 \kappa_q=[q_na_{n,q}]_{n=0}^N.
\]
For a slice morphism $h:(Q,q)\to(Q',q')$, define $B_n(h)$ by
\[
 a_{n,q'}B_n(h)=a_{n,q},\qquad
 b_{n,q'}B_n(h)=h^n b_{n,q}.
\]
Pullback uniqueness proves the identity and composition laws, so
$H(h)=\coprod_nB_n(h)$ defines an endofunctor of $\mathcal D/F$.

uses.paragraph:
Continue with the syntax structure of
Definition~\ref{def:categorical-syntax} and its constructed substitution.
Put $F=\Fm$. The propositional axiom schemes are those of
H\'ajek and Pudl\'ak~\cite[Section 0.10]{HP}:
\begin{align}
 &\varphi\Rightarrow(\psi\Rightarrow\varphi),
                                                        \label{eq:hilbert-one}\\
 &(\varphi\Rightarrow(\psi\Rightarrow\chi))
   \Rightarrow((\varphi\Rightarrow\psi)
   \Rightarrow(\varphi\Rightarrow\chi)),
                                                        \label{eq:hilbert-two}\\
 &(\neg\psi\Rightarrow\neg\varphi)
   \Rightarrow(\varphi\Rightarrow\psi).
                                                        \label{eq:hilbert-three}
\end{align}
The named-variable quantifier axioms follow
Hirst and Hirst~\cite[Sections 2.11--2.12]{HH}; equality is expressed
by reflexivity and substitution of equal terms in formulas
\cite[Section 3.1]{HH}:
\begin{align}
 &(\forall x\,\varphi)\Rightarrow\varphi[x:=t],
                                                        \label{eq:hilbert-instantiation}\\
 &\forall x(\varphi\Rightarrow\psi)
       \Rightarrow(\varphi\Rightarrow\forall x\,\psi),
                                                        \label{eq:hilbert-distribution}\\
 &t=t,                                                   \label{eq:hilbert-reflexivity}\\
 &(u=t)\Rightarrow
       (\varphi[x:=u]\Rightarrow\varphi[x:=t]).           \label{eq:hilbert-equality}
\end{align}
Each scheme denotes a morphism from its parameter object to $F$.
For the first three these objects are $F^2,F^3,F^2$.
For \eqref{eq:hilbert-instantiation}, use the pullback of
$j:\Adm\hookrightarrow F\times V\times\Tm$ along the
permutation $V\times F\times\Tm\to F\times V\times\Tm$.
For \eqref{eq:hilbert-distribution}, use
$[\mem(x,\FV_{\Fm}(\varphi))=\mathbf{f}]
\hookrightarrow V\times F^2$.
For \eqref{eq:hilbert-reflexivity}, use $\Tm$.
For \eqref{eq:hilbert-equality}, intersect the pullbacks of $j$
along
\[
 (x,\varphi,u,t)\longmapsto(\varphi,x,u),\qquad
 (x,\varphi,u,t)\longmapsto(\varphi,x,t)
\]
from $V\times F\times\Tm^2$ to $F\times E$.
Let $L$ be the coproduct of these seven parameter objects and
$\lambda:L\to F$ their copairing.

In $(\mathcal D/E)^2$, use the carriers
\[
 X_T=E\times(\Tm\times\Tm)\longrightarrow E,
 \qquad
 X_F=E\times(\Fm\times O(\Fm))\longrightarrow E.
\]
The first component of each pair records the original expression.
Retaining this component obtains structural recursion from initial-algebra
iteration; compare Gabbay and Pitts~\cite[proof of Corollary 6.7]{GabbayPitts}.
Define a $K_E$-algebra as follows, retaining the same parameter
$(x,t)$ in every operation. At a variable $v$, the pair is
\[
 (\eta v,\mathsf{if}(\epsilon(v,x);t,\eta v)).
\]
At a function symbol, apply its constructor separately to the
original term components and the substituted term components.
At equality and relation symbols, reconstruct the original formula
and apply $\ok_{\Fm}$ to the formula formed from the substituted
term components. At negation and implication, reconstruct the
original formula and apply $O(\neg)$ or
$\widehat{\Rightarrow}$ to the result components.

For an endofunctor on the $r$-fold product category $\mathcal D^r$
defined using finite products, coproducts, and specified constant objects, its version on

by replacing each constant $X$ by $P\times X\to P$ and using
products and coproducts in that slice. An initial algebra is
\emph{stable under parameters} if, for every $P\in\mathcal D$,
its pullback along $P\to1$ is initial for this slice endofunctor.

Cockett~\cite{CockettLists}; its formulation by pullback into slices is
recalled by Maietti~\cite[Definition 2.4 and the following paragraph]{MaiettiLists}.

uses.paragraph:
The relation between split ranges and factorizations through restriction
monomorphisms is developed in Cockett, Guo, and
Hofstra~\cite[Theorem 4.7 and Lemma 4.12]{CGHRangeI}.
The additional conditions for these to be regular-image factorizations
are given in \cite[Section 3.16 and Proposition 3.17]{CGHRangeII}.

The partial-map category $\Par(\mathcal D,\Mono)$ has morphisms given
by spans with monic left leg, composed by pullback
\cite[Section 3]{CockettLack}. Since $\mathcal D$ is regular, it is a
split restriction category with ranges
\cite[Theorem 4.5 and Section 4.11]{CGHRangeI}; its total subcategory
is canonically isomorphic to $\mathcal D$.
The sentence theory is represented in this category by
\[
 t_A=[S\xleftarrow{m_A}T_{A,S}\xrightarrow{m_A}S]:S\rightharpoonup S,
 \qquad m_A:T_{A,S}\hookrightarrow S.
\]
Every monomorphism in $\mathcal D$ has a partial inverse in this
partial-map category. Lemma~\ref{lem:range-regular-image} therefore
gives $t_A=\ran(c_{A,S})$.
If instead $\mathcal D=\Tot(\Split(\mathcal R))$ for a restriction
category $\mathcal R$ whose restriction splitting has ranges, require
$m_A$ to have a partial inverse
$r_A:S\rightharpoonup T_{A,S}$ in $\Split(\mathcal R)$.
The same lemma gives
\[
 \ran(c_{A,S})=m_A r_A=\bar r_A.
\]
Thus the range represents the constructed sentence theory.
